title: Read the Answer Twice: Separate Claim from Wording
body:
An AI answer has two layers: the claims it makes, and the confident wording that carries them. Confident wording is not evidence, and a well-written paragraph can carry a false claim as smoothly as a true one. Reading twice separates the layers: the first read is for understanding, the second read is for listing, in your own words, exactly what is being claimed, so that each claim can be checked on its own.

How to do it: Read the answer once for understanding; Read it again and list each claim in your own words; Mark which claims matter for your decision and which are decoration; Set aside claims you cannot yet check, rather than assuming them; Check the decision-relevant claims first.

What to check: After listing claims, ask whether any claim changed meaning when you restated it. If restating a claim makes it vaguer or stronger, the original wording was doing work that evidence had not done.

When to stop or get help: Do not act on an answer whose decision-relevant claims you cannot verify. Use it as a draft to investigate, not as a conclusion.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

claims = ['date', 'amount', 'name', 'rule']
checked = ['date', 'amount']
print('claims listed:', len(claims))
print('claims checked:', len(checked))
print('unverified claims:', [c for c in claims if c not in checked])

claims listed: 4
claims checked: 2
unverified claims: ['name', 'rule']

title: Ask for Sources, Then Open Them Yourself
body:
A source list at the end of an AI answer is a lead, not a verification. AI systems can invent plausible-looking citations, link to pages that do not support the claim, or summarise a real source inaccurately. Opening the source yourself, finding the relevant passage, and confirming it says what the answer says it says is the step that turns a citation into evidence.

How to do it: Ask the AI which source supports each key claim; Open each source yourself, not through a summary; Find the exact passage that supports the claim; Check the source's date, author, and authority for this topic; Note where no source supports a claim, even if sources are listed.

What to check: If a source cannot be opened, is behind a wall you cannot cross, or does not contain the passage, treat the claim as unverified. A citation you cannot inspect is not stronger than no citation.

When to stop or get help: Do not quote or forward a sourced claim you have not opened. If the source matters, the extra minutes of opening it are part of using the answer responsibly.

title: Cross-Check Numbers: Recompute, Do Not Re-Quote
body:
Numbers are the easiest AI claims to check and the easiest to get wrong by copying. A total, a percentage, a conversion, or a date difference can be recomputed with ordinary arithmetic, a calculator, or a spreadsheet, and recomputation catches both arithmetic slips and wrong starting figures. Re-quoting a number in a new document does not check it; doing the sum again does.

How to do it: Write down the starting figures the answer used; Recompute the result yourself with a calculator or spreadsheet; Check units, currencies, and date ranges match; Compare your result with the answer's result digit by digit; Investigate any difference, however small, before using the number.

What to check: If your recomputation differs, trust your arithmetic until you find the error, and check whether the answer used a different starting figure, a different year, or a rounded value without saying so. Rounding that is not disclosed is itself a finding.

When to stop or get help: Do not use a number in a decision, a payment, or a published document until it recomputes cleanly from figures you have seen yourself.

title: Dates, Names, and Quotes Are the First Things to Verify
body:
Dates, names, and quotations are high-risk details in AI answers because they look precise while being easy to invent: a wrong year, a misspelled name, or a quotation that was never said can pass unnoticed inside an otherwise sound answer. They are also the easiest details to verify, because a name or a date can be searched directly against a primary or authoritative source. Checking them first gives a fast signal about the whole answer's reliability.

How to do it: List every date, name, and quotation in the answer; Search each one directly against an authoritative source; Check spelling of names character by character; Check quotations word by word, including who said them and when; Treat a quotation with no findable source as unverified, however apt it sounds.

What to check: If one date or quotation proves wrong, raise your checking level for the rest of the answer. A single invented detail does not prove everything is wrong, but it proves the answer was not checked before it reached you.

When to stop or get help: Do not publish or repeat a quotation, date, or name from an AI answer until you have found it in a source you trust. Attribution is a claim, and claims need sources.

title: If It Sounds Too Certain, Ask What It Does Not Know
body:
AI answers often sound certain even when the evidence is thin, disputed, or missing, because the style of a fluent answer hides the gaps in its knowledge. Asking what is unknown, what is disputed, and what would change the answer forces those gaps into the open. A good answer to a hard question names its limits; an answer that cannot name any limit is a warning, not a strength.

How to do it: Ask what evidence would change the answer; Ask what experts disagree about on this topic; Ask what the answer does not cover; Ask for the confidence of each key claim separately; Treat a claim with no stated limit as a claim to check hardest.

What to check: Compare the stated limits with what you know: if a topic you know is disputed is presented as settled, the answer's certainty is a style choice, not a measurement.

When to stop or get help: Do not act on a single certain-sounding answer for a disputed, medical, legal, or financial question. Seek a second, independent source before deciding.

title: Copy, Test, and Run Code Claims Before Trusting Them
body:
Code in an AI answer is a claim that can be tested exactly: run it, in a safe place, with known inputs, and compare the output with what the answer promises. Code that looks correct can fail on edge cases, use a library you do not have, or quietly do something different from its description. Running it turns a reading task into an experiment, and the experiment settles the question.

How to do it: Copy the code into a safe test environment, never straight into a production system; Run it with small, known inputs first; Compare the actual output with the promised output; Test edge cases such as empty input and large input; Read the code for actions you did not ask for, such as deleting files or sending data.

What to check: If the code fails, changes data, or needs permissions you did not expect, stop and investigate before fixing it by hand. A fix that makes it run is not proof it was right.

When to stop or get help: Do not run AI-generated code on real data, real accounts, or a shared system until it has passed tests on safe sample data.

title: The Independent Second Path
body:
An independent second path is a different way to reach the same answer: a different method, a different source, or a different calculation, chosen so that an error in the first path cannot silently pass through the second. Asking the same AI the same question again is not a second path, because the same error can repeat. Independence is the point: if two genuinely different routes agree, confidence rises for a reason, not from repetition.

How to do it: Solve or check the problem by a second, different method; Use a source that does not copy the first source; Compare the two results in detail, not just the headline; Investigate any disagreement before choosing a result; Record both paths so someone else can repeat them.

What to check: If the two paths disagree, do not pick the one you prefer. Find the step where they diverge, and check that step against a third source or by hand.

When to stop or get help: Do not treat agreement between two copies of the same answer as verification. Copies agree because they are copies.

title: Spot a Hallucinated Citation
body:
A hallucinated citation is a reference that looks scholarly but does not exist, or exists but says something different from what the answer claims. It is persuasive precisely because checking it takes effort: a journal name, a year, and a page range feel authoritative at a glance. The check is mechanical: search the title, the authors, and the journal separately, and confirm the work exists and supports the claim.

How to do it: Search the work's title exactly; Search the authors and the journal separately; Confirm the year, volume, and pages match a real publication; Open the work or its abstract and find the claimed passage; Treat a citation that cannot be found in any catalogue as invented until proven otherwise.

What to check: If the work exists but the passage does not support the claim, the citation is misused, not merely mistyped. Note the difference, because it changes how much of the answer to trust.

When to stop or get help: Do not cite a reference in your own work until you have found it yourself. Passing on an invented citation spreads the error under your name.

title: Check Images and Media Claims Against Original Context
body:
Images and media in or behind an AI answer can be misattributed, outdated, cropped, or generated, while the answer presents them as evidence for a current event or a specific place. Checking an image means checking its original context: where it first appeared, when it was made, and what it actually shows, rather than what the caption claims. A reverse image search and a look at the original publication are ordinary, quick checks.

How to do it: Find where the image first appeared; Check its date and place against the claim; Look for cropping that changes the meaning; Check whether the image is generated, stock, or from a different event; Compare the caption with what the image itself shows.

What to check: If the image cannot be traced to an original, treat it as unproven illustration, not as evidence. An untraceable image cannot support a factual claim, however vivid it is.

When to stop or get help: Do not share an image as evidence for an event until its original context matches the claim. Sharing is republishing, and the error travels with your name.

title: Compare Two Independent Sources, Not Two Copies of One
body:
Two web pages that agree are not two independent confirmations if one copied the other, both quote the same press release, or both summarise the same AI answer. Independence means different authors, different evidence, and different routes to the conclusion. Finding genuine independence takes a little digging: check publication dates, authors, and the evidence each source actually cites, and be suspicious when two sources use identical wording.

How to do it: Identify the evidence each source cites; Check authors, dates, and publishers for each; Look for identical wording that suggests copying; Prefer sources that gathered their own evidence; Treat two copies as one source, however many pages repeat them.

What to check: If both sources trace back to a single press release or a single study, your confirmation count is one, not two. Say so plainly when you report the claim.

When to stop or get help: Do not present copied agreement as independent confirmation in your own writing. Count sources by their evidence, not by their number.

title: Verify Health, Legal, and Money Advice With a Qualified Source
body:

title: Build a Verification Checklist for a Whole Report
body:
A whole report needs a checklist, because checking claims one by one without a plan lets the most important claims hide among the easiest ones. A checklist ranks claims by decision importance, assigns a check method to each, and records the result: verified, unverified, or contradicted. When the checklist is complete, you can say honestly which parts of the report you stand behind and which parts remain open, instead of giving the whole report a single vague stamp.

How to do it: List every decision-relevant claim in the report; Rank claims by how much your decision depends on them; Assign each claim a check method: source, recomputation, second path, or expert; Record verified, unverified, or contradicted for each; Summarise the open claims before deciding.

What to check: Review the checklist with a second person where the decision matters. A fresh pair of eyes catches claims the first checker stopped seeing.

When to stop or get help: Do not approve a report whose top-ranked claims remain unverified. Approve the verified parts, and mark the rest as open work.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. title: Detect Overgeneralization and Missing Conditions
body:
Overgeneralization is when a true statement about some cases is presented as true about all cases, and missing conditions are the limits that were quietly dropped: for whom, where, when, and under what conditions the claim holds. AI answers are prone to both, because a general-sounding sentence reads better than a careful one. Restoring the conditions is a verification skill: ask who the claim covers, where it was tested, and what exceptions exist.

How to do it: Restate the claim with its conditions: who, where, when, and under what conditions; Ask for exceptions and counterexamples; Check whether the evidence covers the group you belong to; Look for words such as always, never, and everyone, and test them; Rewrite the claim in its narrow, supported form before using it.

What to check: If the narrow form is much weaker than the original, the original was doing the persuading, not the evidence. Use the narrow form.

When to stop or get help: Do not apply a general claim to yourself or your group until you have checked that the conditions cover you. A claim true for one group can be false for another.

title: Verify Translations and Multilingual Answers
body:
Translation errors in AI answers are quiet: a word translated plausibly but wrongly, a polite form turned rude, or a number or date shifted by a format difference can change meaning without looking wrong. Checking a translation means checking it backwards and with a speaker of the language where it matters: translate it back, compare the meaning, and confirm names, numbers, and dates survived unchanged.

How to do it: Translate the answer back into the original language and compare meanings; Check names, numbers, dates, and addresses character by character; Ask a speaker of the language to check passages that matter; Check polite and formal forms fit the context; Treat machine translation as a draft for important documents, not as a final version.

What to check: If back-translation changes the meaning, the translation is not ready, even if it reads smoothly. Smoothness in the target language is not evidence of fidelity to the source.

When to stop or get help: Do not sign, send, or publish an important translated document on the strength of a single machine translation. A human check is part of the document, not an extra.

title: Audit an AI Agent's Work Before You Approve It
body:
An AI agent that takes actions on your behalf, such as sending messages, changing files, or making bookings, needs an audit before approval, not after the consequences arrive. Auditing means reviewing the log of what it did, checking each action against what you asked, and confirming the results with independent checks. Approval without a log review is not supervision; it is a signature on work you have not seen.

How to do it: Review the agent's action log step by step; Check each action against your original instruction; Confirm results with an independent check, such as opening the file or message sent; Revoke or narrow permissions that were broader than needed; Keep the log with your approval decision.

What to check: If any action falls outside your instruction, treat the whole run as suspect until that action is explained. One unexplained action can hide others.

When to stop or get help: Do not approve agent work that changed money, messages, files, or accounts without reviewing the log. If you cannot see the log, do not approve the run.

title: Teach Verification: A Routine for Home and Classroom
body:
Teaching verification is teaching a routine, not a lecture about truth: a short, repeatable set of steps that a learner can use on any AI answer, at home or in a classroom. The routine must be short enough to remember, concrete enough to practise, and honest enough to admit when a claim cannot be checked. Learners who practise the routine on easy claims will use it, with help, on hard ones.

How to do it: Teach the routine in five steps: list claims, check sources, recompute numbers, find a second path, and mark what is open; Practise on easy, checkable claims first; Let learners find a wrong AI claim themselves, with guidance; Praise careful checking, not fast answers; Review the routine together after a real, consequential use.

What to check: After teaching, watch learners use the routine without prompting. If they only use it when reminded, the routine is too long or too abstract, and it needs simplifying, not repeating louder.

When to stop or get help: Do not teach verification as distrust of all AI answers. Teach it as the ordinary care that makes good answers usable and bad answers harmless.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed.
